utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you at all the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE APPELLANT: Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, indeed, I can follow the proceedings in my own language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, together with co-counsels Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us today here are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Good morning to you and your team. So do you have any preliminaries that you need to discuss? I suppose there are quite a few. I'm giving you the floor first. I still take it that we are starting with Dr. Gow's testimony today, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With a view to our prior scheme, the latest scheme, there had been a change for this week due to the fact, first, that we had, the Prosecution, will not call the male witness we, in an earlier stage, requested to be on the witness list and had been accepted to be. The female one for the videolink, Ms. Svetlana Trifunovic, I can speak out her name, she doesn't seek for protective measures. That name remains on our list, meaning that we anticipate to have a videolink witness, if everything is in order, for this coming Thursday. The lack -- the space we have, then, on the Friday, we'll try to place in Ms. Racine Manas as a witness. We still have to complete that in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it, recapitulating, that you are dropping one of the two witnesses that we are supposed to hear by videolink, and that you're retaining only one. You're bringing the testimony of that person, Svetlana Trifunovic from Friday, 26th to Thursday, 25th --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. To Thursday, the 25th. And that you are filling, then, Friday, 26th, with the testimony of Racine Manas. Is that agreeable to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that on Monday, the 29th, we will not be sitting. I had told you that already. I am pleased to inform everyone that, during these two weeks' break that we have had, a lot, a lot of work has been done by my staff. Not only by my staff, also I notice that you've had an opportunity, both the Prosecution and the Defence, to reorganise yourself, and it shows that sometimes a short break is conducive to a better handling and a more efficient way of handling the case. Now, I'm pretty sure that the case will actually even be shortened as we go along. In any case, we have got now all the system of exhibits, documents, well catalogued and preserved, and we have also started working on the various other issues, particularly legal matters involved in this case, so that when we come to the final stage of this case, we will have practically everything ready and we could then be in a position to proceed at quite a pace. I am also informed that there were some new filings, and I appreciate your enthusiasm in making sure that the three Judges are fully occupied with such matters. There are two filings in particular that I think, having gone through them -- I must admit that I have not yet had the chance to sit down with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser to even discuss the subject matter of these motions, but I'm sure that when we do later on today, we are going to agree that they require some kind of debate, both of them. Not just one or the other, I think both of them require some kind of debate. So I would like you to discuss amongst yourselves and identify a day when you could debate these two outstanding new motions. We will be discussing them in-camera as well. But I would like you to inform us when you need -- yes, Mr. Di Fazio, I see. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, if you please. I'm grateful for you clarifying those issues. Do I take it then that you want, the Chamber wants, oral submissions on either of those two motions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the case. Both motions are such. One of it is a sort of, not exactly a follow-up, but it does follow up from matters that we discussed in the pre-trial stage and also at the beginning of the trial. That seems to call for some kind of either a revision of the situation. But in any case, I think some oral submissions will be in place. MR. DI FAZIO: Respectfully, we agree, and in fact prefer to take that course. I'd like to address Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'd like you to do, I usually work it out this way, is to see if you can agree on a day in which -- and time frame in which you could make these submissions, and then you just let us know, we will have the oral pleadings or the debate, say, on Wednesday, and we require one hour. And we'll make the necessary adjustments then accordingly, all right? Good. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: It is Wednesday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I just ask you to discuss it with -- I just ask you to discuss it with -- I just mentioned Wednesday, just like that. MR. DI FAZIO: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As an example. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. In addition, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that we sent a letter to the Defence in which we sent them a medical opinion of the specialist in Sarajevo, as requested in the 92 bis procedure. And attached to that letter, you also find a draft English translation of the conclusion. We don't -- we were not able yet in this stage to file a complete translation, and we are working on it. But we already send a draft translation, and as soon as we have the translation of it, we will file the supplement information to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I thank you. The only thing I can say is that the only information that I have for the time being is that there has been some development. I haven't seen the letter. And I suppose, will I see it, then I should be in a position -- oh, we have it here. Okay. Let me just have a look at it. In the meantime, I notice that Madam Vidovic asked for the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did receive the Sarajevo expert opinion, and we now agree to apply Rule 92 bis to this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think the matter, at this point in time, can be decided by us. I don't think it requires any further discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, for the record, it needs anyhow to confirm the final conclusion of the specialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the final conclusion is -- I have only got one paragraph here which supposedly translates point 5 of the certification by Dr. Lubovic, and says answering specifically questions from the memo: "I am of the opinion that X is not fit to give testimony in a trial and answer questions pertaining to events which occurred more than 10 years ago, nor can it be expected that his overall health would improve and that preconditions will be met at a certain time to make him fit to testify in the said trial." So at that point in time, I think there's only one thing remaining to be done, taking into consideration of what has just been mentioned by Ms. Vidovic, and that is to decide your motion to have his prior statement, or whatever, admitted under Rule 92, whatever, (C), 92 bis (C). And we will do that -- we will do that this week. There are other things that we are working upon, but this shouldn't take us much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted) No, the rest is points for our consideration. Having said that, if you have no further initial, preliminary matters to raise, we will admit Dr. Gow into the courtroom and we will start with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. I am the presiding judge. My name is Judge Agius. I'm flagged on my right by Judge Brydensholt from Denmark, on my left, Judge Eser from Germany. We welcome you. You're about to give expert evidence, or as an expert witness for the Prosecution in this case against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you do so you enter a solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath, that during the course of your testimony, you'll be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please read that text out loud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, you can lead the witness in the first part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's what I was going to ask permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would the witness please state his full name and title for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: My name is Andrew James William Gow, and I am professor of international peace and security at King's College London.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you also describe for the Trial Chamber what is your field of study.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I teach, research and write on war, that is, on problems of international politics, of strategy, military/political affairs. And I've spent quite a lot of time over the past 15 or more years dealing with the former Yugoslavia, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. During this past 15 years, have you published articles, manuscripts or books in your field of study, being peace and security as applied to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I have. I've published a number of books, three single-authored books, as well as a number of co-authored books, and I've published a number of articles that I don't even remember, but into the tens of articles on the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that in the future I will submit Dr. Gow's expert report which contains also his writings, and so therefore I will not belabour that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to do that, unless the matter is being contested by the Defence. Okay. You may proceed, Ms. Sellers, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Also, Dr. Gow, have you lectured on peace and security as it applied to the former Yugoslavia, and if so, name maybe a couple of those places.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I've lectured, given talks, participated in discussions and events in a large number of places in Europe, in North America, universities of Oxford, Cambridge. I've held visiting positions at the universities of Princeton and Columbia in the United States. I've given lectures all around universities in the United Kingdom and at several places in the United States again as well, in Boston, St. Louis, Indianapolis. I can keep going.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I would take it that in addition to travelling through Europe and North America, that you have made several visits to the former Yugoslavia, is that correct, sir, for the purposes of your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: For most of the past 20 years, I was going to the former Yugoslavia a few times a year. In the last three or four years, that's generally come down a bit. But I've been going still a couple times a year, primarily to Serbia. But I've been around all the region over the whole of that period, and I've also given lectures and talks and so forth within that region, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In addition to research about issues in the former Yugoslavia, your travels to the region, have you spoken and exchanged ideals and information with other professionals in your field about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Oh, yes. As part of researching and writing, I talk to people from the region, from outside the region, academics, officials, legible people. One carries out interviews, has conversations with people over the years. Yeah, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have they all informed you in terms of your research and your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I find that almost anything I do informs me in terms of research and study. It's hard not to. But yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you, what is the title of your latest book that deals with the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: "The Serbian Project and its Adversaries: A Strategy of War Crimes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when was that book published?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Last year, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how would you characterise that book, "The Serbian Project" in terms of this field of study in which you've been engaged in in the past 15 years?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's an attempt to capture the essence of the strategic aspects of the war. It's looking at the link between strategy and war crimes, and, in doing so, is attempting to capture the way in which the Serbian strategy, which I say is, without trying to produce anything else in the book, predicated on acts that could be described as war crimes, was the core to a war of dissolution about statehood, but the adversaries recognising that adversaries had competing strategies with the local adversaries or international, and that sometimes local adversaries also adopted the same strategy as well, or elements of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. We'll return to your book throughout the giving of your evidence. But I would like to ask you, have you testified at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have you testified in cases where Muslims were the victims of alleged Serb crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what case was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: That's a trial in the case of Dusko Tadic, which was the first trial to come to court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have you also testified in cases where Serbs were the victims of alleged Muslim crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what case was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: That was in the case of Delalic, et al, Celebici, the Celebici case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber about the political composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the years that just preceded 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia comprised six states within a state. The federal state had independent international personality, for purposes of international law, but within that there were six states, each defined constitutionally as sovereign. So in theory, they were exercising -- the exercise of sovereign rights was transferred to the whole. The six states were, working from north to south, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, which comprised two historic regions, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. Within Serbia, there were also two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo, which had de jure powers but were seen as sort of sovereignty within that arrangement. Each of those operated as a whole but operated as separate political entities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you'd notice, there's a map to your right. I would ask that you use the pointer, and what you've just described to Your Honours, would you please point to those six republics, and I would like to ask the AV unit if you would focus your cameras on the map so we might have a display of that image on our monitors, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Am I allowed to stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I ask the AV unit to focus on the map so we might see it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In the north, the north-west, Slovenia; Croatia is kind of broken goose-shape along the coast and through the mainland; Bosnia and Herzegovina, the heart-shaped country in the middle; Serbia, running from the north down the eastern side here; Montenegro in the southwest -- southwest of Serbia, south of Bosnia; and Macedonia in the very south, bordering beyond it into Greece and to west Albania and the east Bulgaria. The two provinces I mentioned, Vojvodina, is in the north, primarily the green bit on the north of this bit of the map of Serbia, and Kosovo is in down in the south, approximately somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel and the witness please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For the purposes of this case, could you please also show Your Honours on the map the location of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And could you please also show Your Honours, for purposes of this case, the borderline between Serbia and Bosnia where the Drina river is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: As you say, the Drina river forms the border, and it runs here [indicates]. Serbia lies to the east, Bosnia and Herzegovina to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And lastly, could you show Your Honours, for the purposes of this case, where the region of Srebrenica is in what you've just described.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's Eastern Bosnia, somewhere in the region of here. There it is. Srebrenica is on this map. It's just there, so this area, in the middle pocket to the west of the river, just there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, Dr. Gow. Your Honours, I would just like to note that we have presented the map just for purposes of display. We do not intend to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I took it for granted, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you now please tell the Trial Chamber what was the ethnic composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It was mixed. The two single largest ethnic groups were Serbs who comprised somewhere in the mid-30s, 36 per cent in the 1981 census, 34 per cent in the 1991 census, which is not necessarily accepted by all parties. The second largest group were Croats, just under 20 per cent. And then there were Slav Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegrins, Macedonians, and Albanians, each of which comprised somewhere 6 to 10 per cent of the population. In addition to that, there were a number of very small groups, Czechs, Slovaks; Ukrainians, a larger number, who made up parts of the population, and about 5 per cent who defined themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there any one ethnic group wholly contained or that resided in just one of the republics that you've described on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: No. No ethnic group was contained within any one of the political units. The most homogeneous was Slovenia, which had a little over 90 per cent in the population, but there were Slovenes outside. The province of Kosovo was also said to be in the region of 90 per cent ethnically homogeneous. Apart from that, the figure for Croatia was about three-quarters ethnic Croats, but Croats outside in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serbs comprised about two-thirds of the population of Serbia, although if you take out Serbia without the provinces, that went up to about 85 per cent. The Macedonians, Montenegrins, each about two-thirds of the population. And Bosnia and Herzegovina was more divided with about 44 per cent Slav Muslims, 31 or so per cent ethnic Serbs, and about 17 per cent ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please pause between questions and answers. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: If I may add, I don't know if it's assistance to Your Honours. But given that there was a camera closing up in the map before, if they are interested, this map that's been displayed also has a pattern of ethnic distribution in the bottom left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber what were the principal languages spoken in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The principal languages, constitutional languages, were Serbian, Serbo-Croat, which was spoken by about 80 per cent of the population, Serbs, Croats, and the Slav Muslim populations and the Montenegrins. And also Slovene spoken by Slovenes and Macedonian spoken by Macedonians. Those were distinct but related, philologically related languages. And in addition, you have the ethnic Albanians which speak -- spoke Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while we are at this and the witness referred to the map in a more specific way, could we have an indication as to which period that map refers to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the pre-war period or is it the post-war?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the pre-war period, the composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I imagined so, but I wanted it to be so stated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you, what were the principal religions of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The Orthodox Christianity practiced predominantly by Serbs in Serbia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, by Montenegrins, and by Macedonians. Roman Catholicism practiced predominantly by Slovenes, ethnic Croats in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and by some Albanians in Montenegro. And Islam practiced by Slav Muslims, so ethnically the same you would say as Croats and Serbs, but practising Islamic faith, and by the ethnically distinct group of Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, we've talked about the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Did that republic disintegrate politically in the beginning of the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: May I have now the map. I don't know if you're interested in looking at the map at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why we have the map on the monitor. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We do not need the map on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think we need the map any further. Please proceed, Dr. Gow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the 1990s, this Yugoslav federation dissolved; it broke up. That was the result of a set of political, social, economic pressures, international change, through the 1980s. It broke up in a way where, because of the structures of this unit, with the six states within a state seeking -- being obliged to operate together, in theory, for their own benefit, they couldn't agree on the way forward. And as the disputes deepened, the federation, in a sense, ceased to function, so that there came a point in the middle of 1991, as a result of a series of events through 1990 and 1991, where, at the political level, the interstate, inter-republican level, there was no agreement, and two of those states, Slovenia and Croatia, decided to declare independence at the same time at which other states were trying to evaluate their positions and had been working out what they also would do. And, of course, in this context, there was also quite a lot of pressure in the ethnic social fabric running through the states and across the borders of those states.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I'd like to ask you to explain a bit about -- you testified that there was ethnic tension and a series of events. Could you just illuminate that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In terms of tension in the ethnic fabric, it was quite clear that, as the end of communism affected Europe and the move towards democratisation in some -- eventually in some ways all of those Yugoslav states. The move to democracy opened discussion on national issues in a different way and in a new way. For example, in Croatia, that created tensions within the ethnic Serb communities there. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, in this context, predominantly ethnically defined political parties emerged and ethnic groups tended to lend their support to their ethnic party. This didn't necessarily imply that there had to be mutually exclusive positions which would lead to conflict. At times in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it appeared at times as all parties were cooperating together. In retrospect, we don't know quite how to evaluate that. But those pressures were taking place. In terms of the interstate relations, Slovenia, supported by Croatia, proposed a realignment of the joint arrangement, confirming the sovereignty of the states, taking -- giving greater authority within that arrangement to the states in exercising their own affairs internationally. They had substantial control internally. Serbian authorities in Belgrade countered with a proposal not to loosen relations, to make them more comfortable, but to tighten them. These were mutually exclusive positions. And so through a series of events, it became clear that there was probably no way in which they were going to be able to go forward together on that basis. In that context, in the spring of -- I mean in late 1990, Slovenia held a referendum; in the spring of 1991, Croatia held a referendum on the issue of independence, if a way forward was not found. These events contributed to the dynamic between the parties about what was going on and how it was going to turn out. And by the time it came to change the -- what was called technically the president of the presidency, that is, the head of the state council -- if you think of an image - I don't know if it helps to think of the European Union, where you have the European Council where all the heads of state come together - the equivalent of that body in this Yugoslav construct was due to change its presidency, the person, the titular head of it. But that was blocked by Serbia. And at that moment, the logjam was set, and it was only about -- a little over a month after that that the declarations of independence came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I'd like to ask you, some of the events surrounding the declarations of independence that you've testified about, did they include the intervention of any armed forces on the part of republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Throughout the period in which these -- the kinds of tensions I was describing, both at the interstate, political level and within the communal fabric, from the middle of 1990 onwards, there were rebellious regions controlled by ethnic Serbs within Croatia which were using arms to create effective no-go areas for the Croatian authorities. They were, in some ways, supported by elements of the then Yugoslav People's Army. This was all part of the evolving situation. And within that context, also, Slovenia began preparing to have a -- to use armed forces that it already had, but to enhance them for the purposes of being able to promote its position, to defend its position, if it came to that. And of course, when the -- at the moment the declarations of independence were made, war began.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And therefore, did the Yugoslav People's Army at a time physically intervene on the territory of these republics, and then later on at another point in time, withdraw of these republics, Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: To be accurate, because the Yugoslav People's Army Yugoslav People's Army was the army of the federation, it was always present in all of the territories. At times in 1990 it was deployed out of barracks at places within Croatia as part of this tense, potential conflict, or actual conflict, but low-level conflict situation. After the point of the declarations of independence, it was deployed technically to assist the civilian authorities by moving to suppress the Slovenian and Croatian declarations of independence. At a later stage, after 10 days of armed hostilities and a three-month moratorium, it withdrew completely from Slovenia. It was only to withdraw -- well, no, sorry, difficult issues. The forces that it became were to withdraw eventually from Croatia in 19 -- after 1995, but the JNA ceased to exist as such in 1992. But that's an issue you probably don't want to get into just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll talk about that a bit later.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to assist us. I'm turning to number 1 in our binder. The Prosecution has provided binders of the different exhibits that we're using, and if she would kindly pass out what's under page Exhibit 1. Everyone has it now? Dr. Gow, it's your number 0039405 in the original Slovenian, and it is 15 in the English version. I believe it's up on our monitor of court evidence. Dr. Gow, would you please look at the English version of this. What does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: This is the declaration of independence by the Slovenian parliament, which was made on the 20th of June, 1991. It makes reference to the right to self-determination, and it makes -- and it indicates that Slovenia, in the situation where the federation is no longer functioning, is going to seek its own future as an independent political entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that the document be given a P number, and I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit P408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that document -- I see no objection on the part of the Defence. That document is being admitted in evidence and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P408. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now I would like you to turn to number 2 in the binder the Prosecution's provided, and I would ask the usher, would you please show the witness -- oh, he has -- you've given him the binder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I have the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That makes it much easier.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I've also worked out how to operate this thing, so I can see the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you go to ERN number 00328704, the original. Then I would like to ask Dr. Gow to look at the English version of the document. And that's ERN number 00328704 through 8707. Dr. Gow, could you please tell me what this document represents.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document, as a whole, is taken from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, and if you move to the document numbered 875 within - I think it's 875 within this - you have the declaration of independence by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I might assist you, that's -- excuse me, on page 6 of 14.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's page 6 of 14 of the -- of that document. This document was also promulgated on the 25th of June, 1991, although I should -- I point out that when this was shown to me yesterday, I noted that, for some reason, the translation on this particular version says 25th of May, which is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honours and the Defence to look at page 10 of 14 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow has testified that -- you note that it says May as opposed to saying June. Dr. Gow, your testimony is that the declaration of independence occurred at June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, the Prosecution has sought the assistance of an English-Croatian dictionary so that one might look at the original word in Croatian to verify that the word as translated in English appears to be incorrect. What is May should be June. Could I please hand out these copies. In the document of the original Croatian, and I would ask you to turn to the page which has ERN number 00328707, if you would notice in the first column, about four lines down it says "Zagreb 25," and I would ask you to excuse my mispronunciation pronunciation, "Lipnja" as the month, and then I would direct Your Honours to that same word in the dictionary. It is on page 627, in the first column, approximately seven words from the bottom. And it says that that word would be translated to June. What the Prosecution would like to propose is that we give the document to Language Services and have them correct it for us officially. But I would want to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement on that on the part of the Defence? Because then we can agree that the proper date and the proper translation should have been June, and that we do not need to proper the Translation Unit with making any further adjustments. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the correct translation of the word "Lipnja" is June, and I agree with what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask what is the correct translation of the month of May into Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Svibanj," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no real reasonable explanation for the mistake. It's just a mistake and that's it. I don't think we need to pursue it any further, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful to Your Honours and I'm grateful to our learned friends. I would ask that we tender the exhibit into evidence, if I could have a P number for it, please. And that would be documents relating to the Croatian independence. And if Your Honours feel necessary, then I will not have to tender the dictionary pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to tender this into evidence. The other one should be 409.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's exact. That would be P409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the document relating to the Croatian declaration of independence is being admitted in evidence and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P409. And we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would now ask you to turn your attention to the following: How did the independence of Slovenia and Croatia in 1991 affect the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other republic of Serbia and those that made up part of the federation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Would you mind if I added something to the matter of the declarations of independence first?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, certainly, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It was just to make clear that the context of those, and both the declarations made reference to the constitutional position within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which, in the preamble, gave the right to secession, self-summation up to and including secession, and to elements of the constitution Article 3 which defined them as sovereign. And although Article 5 was a co-mitigating factor saying there had to be agreement on change of territory or borders, that didn't necessarily say anything about status. And so the assumption was that sovereign rights within this constitutional framework were held by the states to act in that way, to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I would now ask if you could respond to the following question, and that was: How did the independence of Slovenia and Croatia in 1991 affect the other republics, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: While the events between -- predominantly between Slovenia and Croatia on the one hand and Serbia on the other were developing politically, especially when you come to the points of declarations of independence, this creates pressures on Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the most ethnically divided, fragile of these states, and with significant ethnic Serb and Croat populations. The arguments between Croatia and Serbia, in some ways, impact and translate into arguments between ethnic Serbs and ethnic Croats, wherever they happen to be. This puts pressures on political change at the time of democratisation. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it meant that the word developments, such as parliamentary declaration in October 1991 affirming the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina it meant that there were movements by ethnic Serbs and by ethnic Croats looking for union with Serbia or to reject the declarations of sovereignty, and those pressures meant that the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the predominantly Slav Muslim authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as time went on, took the decision that the best interests of protecting Bosnia and Herzegovina - and I suspect particularly the Slav Muslims within that - would be also to move for a declaration of independence. I think they were reluctant to do that because of the fragile situation. But when the European Council, the governing body as it was of the European Union, in December 1991, invited those Yugoslav and Soviet states seeking recognition of independent international personality to submit requests, applications to do so, Bosnia and Herzegovina submitted an application. Am I free to continue on that or would you rather I didn't?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, when you make a pause, I was going to then ask you: It's your evidence, your expert opinion, that the ethnic and the religious composition of the republics did affect the dissolution or disintegration of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The dissolution was operating at a political level between the governments, but there was tension in the ethnic fabric which both contributed to that process and, in some way, was a product of it. Tension was growing all around. And in a place like Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were pressures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did Bosnia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, eventually declare its independence from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, after the European Council invited those Yugoslav and Soviet states seeking -- the Yugoslav states at that stage in particular, seeking recognition of independent international personality to do so, Bosnia made an application. The European Council, as part of its process of trying to manage the Yugoslav crisis and breakup, had appointed an advisory commission under the French constitutional lawyer, Robert Badinter, and they put each of these cases, including Bosnia and Herzegovina's, to the Badinter Commission, and the Badinter Advisory Commission judged that the will of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not clear and recommended, that a referendum should be held. That referendum was held on the 29th of February, 1st of March, 1991. The outcome of the referendum was that of those who participated, 90 -- almost 90 per cent voted in favour, and that constituted, I think it was about 63 and a half per cent of the population overall. In a later opinion, I think it was opinion number 8, the Badinter Advisory Commission advised the council that Bosnia-Herzegovina, the will of the people had been expressed and that Bosnia and Herzegovina satisfied the terms set in the guidelines and recommended recognition. And the European Council proceeded in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the plebiscite that you mentioned, did the voting in regard to that plebiscite break down, or was it demarcated along ethnic/religious lines, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The voting was predominantly Slav Muslims and Croats voting for independence. Those who voted against -- I'm not sure we can be sure. But there was a boycott organised by the largest Serbian political party, the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, which also, with the assistance of some JNA units, made it difficult even for some people to vote in the referendum. It should also be pointed out, as the Badinter Advisory Commission noted that the previous autumn, in November, the Bosnian Serbs had organised a plebiscite of their own among the ethnic Serbs which expressed their -- as far as you can take it as signifying anything, expressed the view that the ethnic Serbs in Bosnia wanted to remain part of the Federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Sellers, I just suggest that for practical purposes, we -- because I've noticed that you have used the word "plebiscite" with reference to what the witness had previously referred to, mentioned as -- described as referendum. More or less, I would suggest that you restrict the use of plebiscite only to the Serbian plebiscite --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- while we continue to refer to the referendum on whether Bosnia should become independent or not as the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll keep the two separate, even though basically there isn't much difference. But we'll keep the two terms separate, referring to two different events or two different expressions of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for the fine and important distinction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, now, was there a Serbian reaction to Bosnia's declaration of independence that came from, at this point, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In the context of these developments, the Serbian authorities in Belgrade, who by this stage had already embarked on something that I call in the book this new state project, i.e., to create the borders of a new set of territories, or set of territories essentially for ethnic Serbs from the territories of the states breaking up in Yugoslavia, and that campaign was already underway militarily in Croatia. Preparations for it appear to have been underway through the autumn of 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, in the early part. And as part of that preparation, Slobodan Milosevic, the president of Serbia, in conjunction with Borisav Jovic, the Serbian representative to the federal state council, decided that it would be better if the JNA personnel were redistributed so that all ethnic Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina were based in Bosnia and Herzegovina and non-Bosnian Serbs were based outside. And this was in anticipation of the expected recognition of independent international personality for Bosnia and Herzegovina and their correct understanding, I think, that the continuing presence of the JNA after such recognition would be seen as external interference and, quite possibly, probably an act of aggression. Jovic, therefore, gave instructions to the defence minister, the head of the army, General Veljko Kadijevic, to organise that reorganisation, and Kadijevic by 25th of December reported that it was 90 per cent complete. So this is all part of preparations to deal with this situation. You have the breakup of the socialist federative republic, and you have a set of -- you have a breakup which becomes accompanied by war because there isn't agreement on the successor disposition. There's a clash of statehood projects. Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the others all seeking to preserve territorial integrity of the state and add with sovereignty through this arrangement; Serbia seeking to create a new set of boundaries. And that's the essence of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honours to turn to section 3 in your binder, and it is ERN number 00359513.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please look at this document and tell the Trial Chamber that you've testified to someone referred to as Kadijevic. What is the importance of the documents, if any, that we have placed in this section 3?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document is a translation -- a translated extract from Kadijevic's memoirs. Kadijevic was the defence minister, the head of the army. General Kadijevic, a little time after these events, wrote a memoir, and this particular extract, the bit marked here in italics, indicates the way in which the JNA provided the backbone of the army for the Serbian -- for the so-called Bosnian Serb armed forces. So the JNA, in this process, the old Yugoslav People's Army, made arrangements so that the ethnic -- that as part of this project to change the territorial boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to create a Serbian entity linked to other Serbian entities, that it would then -- that it -- sorry, the aim was to create a Serbian entity linked to other Serbian entities. That would require the use of armed force. The elements of the JNA through this arrangement were used to be the core of that armed force for that purpose. And here, Kadijevic is saying it was the backbone of the Republika Srpska's army, replete with weaponry and equipment. You can read.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, therefore, would it be your testimony, your expert opinion, that the ethnic composition, in particular the Serbian ethnic group, affected, if not drove, many of the decisions that were taken by the JNA at this point in time, 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: There are two things, I think, to be -- to say about the JNA in this situation. The first is that it was traditionally a multiethnic armed force, comprising members of each of the -- of the different communities, but that its officer corps was almost predominantly ethnic Serbian. And in that context, although someone like Kadijevic may in some ways have not been -- certainly wouldn't be regarded by many as really close to Milosevic, it was also a position where the situation of some kind of sense of attachment and loyalty for many people, and also simply the question of the army's having a home and a future, we'll go with that. The other thing -- and so there was a kind of tendency, both for the sake of the army having political support -- every army -- elsewhere in the book Kadijevic says every army needs a home, it needs a state to go with, and in this breakup situation, that was the home that the army -- the army took. The other thing is that it appears that Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic, through his security service, was also having a kind of separate line of chains of command running through, helping to prepare the way to identify people within the JNA who would be -- who would be loyal to this kind of enterprise. So this -- these two trends here, there's not one thing happening in the JNA, but the two trends come together to situate it predominantly -- the rump of the JNA taking its place with the Belgrade political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you describe or inform the Trial Chamber exactly how did the JNA fit into the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia society prior to this time in terms of a military apparatus?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Well, the JNA -- well, first of all, it arose from the success of the communist-led resistance and revolution in the Second World War, so it always had a particular place and standing within communist Yugoslavia, including, at various times, a political status, quite unusually for an armed force. Its function was to be the first of a two-tier defence system. It was meant to be the first echelon of defence. The regular armed forces that if Yugoslavia, the federation, were to be involved, would resist, the idea was for a minimum of 48 hours, while the second tier was mobilised. That second tier was Territorial Defence structures organised at republican and local levels. And the theory of the defence doctrine was the JNA would hold off to provide time for mobilisation. It was assumed that in face of something like a Soviet or NATO attack, the JNA wouldn't be stand up to it indefinitely. But by falling back on a strategy of what we described technically as guerilla tactics, it would be able to offer resistance, and the structures were such that that would go down even to the local levels. So the system was structured so that you would have war presidencies, crisis headquarters, and local armed forces, territorial units, that if they were not able to join up and operate with larger formations, would always operate at the very lowest, even neighbourhood level. So the structures were there, and there would always be some kind of civil military relationship, political authority over whatever armed forces were able to operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So with the Territorial Defence, this unit, this second tier of the two-tier Federal Republic military institution, would it use, as a well-accepted strategy guerilla tactics? Is that your expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The defence doctrine was predicated on a guerilla strategy, and that is the idea that you will not be equivalent in strength in terms of conventional forces. Therefore, you adopt an asymmetric strategy. You're in a weaker position, you use a guerilla approach to seek, to harass, to undermine, to show resistance; in the end to make it, say, unbearable for the invading occupying force to remain. I think you see elements of that in Iraq at the moment, with the same attempts being made. Not that we should talk about that. The idea is that you continue this low-level activity at this scale on your terms rather than trying to meet an enemy on their own terms because you would lose on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would members of the Territorial Defence, as part of at least their theoretical if not their actual training, be advised in the use of this guerilla tactics that you've described as a strategy?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Certainly those that would hold positions of authority would do that, anybody with particular training. Everybody -- every male, that's every able-bodied male, would be a conscript within the JNA, they would then be expected to do reserve duty, including serving as part of Territorial Defence units. There was an assumption that the whole of the population in some way would be mobilised either as part of the Territorial Defence or as what was called civil defence. The civil defence also had training in using small firearms. There would be popular resistance that anybody at any level would be capable of operating that. Everybody would be familiar, I should say, with their particular place in the system, at least to some degree, and that they would have a place. And they would be familiar with what was to be done overall. Those in more leading positions would have greater training in understanding -- in doctrine and how to operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Returning a bit more to the JNA in 1991/'92, I'd like to ask you, was it involved in an armed conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The JNA was involved in an armed conflict in Bosnia, following from the things I was saying earlier. It was the core of the Serbian attempt to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina, to take one -- to take parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that would be linked to both the Republic of Serbian Krajina - that's the territory controlled also with JNA assistance by Serbs in Croatia to the west - and to the east Serbia itself. So the JNA, after this transformation, I think I said that Kadijevic, Jovic and Milosevic between them were involved in creating the situation, the JNA, once the armed hostilities began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was the difference between war and some kind of low-level political violence. That was the armed force which shaped the campaign. The JNA itself ceased to exist formally on the 19th of May, 1992, again, as a result of these changes as foreseen by Milosevic, according to Mr. Jovic, and was divided. It's generally said that it withdrew. What happened was that it was divided. Part of it became the Vojska Yugoslavia, the army of Serbia and Montenegro, and part of it became the Vojska Republika Srpksa, the army of the Bosnian Serbs. But it was a division rather than a withdrawal, and all or most parts of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina became the VRS. There were some elements, some of the more sophisticated aircraft were withdrawn, but other aircraft were left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, we'll return to that in a moment. I would like to ask everyone to turn to section 4 of their binder. There is a map that previously has been given a P number, P366. Dr. Gow, I would like to ask you, did you assist the Office of the Prosecutor back in 1995 in preparing this map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: All I can say is that I might have done. Certainly in summer/autumn of 1994, I asked the Prosecutor's Office to prepare a map of this kind, and I gave them the indications for the information that should be on it. If this version of it came from 1995, that's only a continuation of something that was begun in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Not that I wish to be picky. I just kind of -- yeah, that's a ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please describe for Your Honours exactly the reason for this map, and then illustrate a bit what do some of the designations and highlights on this map mean in terms of your testimony regarding the JNA involvement in the armed conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The map indicates key points of Serbian operations in the first month of armed hostilities; in fact, going slightly back before what's generally recognised as the formal beginning of armed hostilities, in the spring of 1992. It doesn't represent all the places where there were operations or armed hostilities. But what it does show is that there was a pattern within that of ensuring that all key communication points were under Serbian control. So each of these stars represents one of the key pieces -- key points of strategic communications within Bosnia and Herzegovina. You see places like Visegrad. Foca, Visegrad, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bijeljina. These are all places which are significant in terms of access for Serbian forces, if necessary, from Serbia into Bosnia and Herzegovina. The initial -- the first of these operations was at Bosanski Brod, that's in the north, the very top one, on the 27th of March. The war is generally said to have begun in April, but these operations were taking place. That "other operations" across that northern tier are significant in preventing access from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina. So with some operations you're ensuring Serbian access, if necessary, for support, and in others, you're cutting off the entry points for any potential reinforcements from outside. The two -- actually, two other things. The Derventa, and this is something I pointed out in Trial Chambers in the past but I guess it gets forgotten once we go away. It's not actually on the point of communication on the map, but I think you get the idea. And the other is to say that Kupres is the key strategic ground in the whole region. Whoever controls the Kupres heights dominates all the way into central Bosnia and all the way down to the Adriatic coast on the other side. So it's significant that that area was taken earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I would like you to explain where Your Honours might find the Posavina Corridor, if it is located on the map, and what its importance might be.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The town of Brcko in the north-east on the map, where it says Brcko, 30th of April, that's the key town running through the Posavina Corridor. That corridor was the vital link between Serbian-controlled territories in Eastern Bosnia that border Serbia itself, and Serbian-controlled territories in Western Bosnia and through into the Serbian-controlled territories in Croatia. That was the vital link. If this project was to be successful, the territories had to be linked. And that was, if you like, the life-line corridor that kept this project going. At various times there were attempts to widen it, there were attempts to create a broader corridor, initially a second corridor that would lead to a broader corridor, but they failed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Gow, might I ask you were these locations that you've shown on the map, were they places where the JNA army "was successful" in that it dominated the military operation that is shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The JNA provided a significant element in those operations. There were two aspects to the takeover of these places. One was the JNA's operating using its artillery and armour capabilities to surround places. This is part of a general pattern. Other forces, generally we label them as paramilitaries, were then used to go into these places to secure control in conjunction with local forces, local Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence forces, which had been mobilised in the course of the previous autumn and through political action by the Serbian Democratic Party, which from December 1991 had been laying preparations for identifying potential resistance so that people would immediately be identified and perhaps either killed or detained for the new government of the new municipalities under the so-called Serbian label. And within that cooperation within the security centers, i.e., the interior ministry services, and with units of the JNA, and as part of all of that, they were mobilising ethnic Serbs in those areas into Territorial Defence forces also to be part of this. In some cases, it was significant; in other cases, it was perhaps less significant. The key element were the shock troops, which were the paramilitaries, which were provided by -- which, in one way or another, were organised by the Serbian security service from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Dr. Gow, is it your testimony that from the Republic of Serbia, we have not only the JNA army intervening on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also paramilitaries that have come from the Serbian republic intervening and participating in the armed conflict on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: That is my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: And that paramilitary forces, such as those known as the Serbian Volunteer Guard, otherwise known as Arkan's Tigers, involved in the action at Bijeljina for certain were -- they had coordinated with the JNA special -- the JNA units at the Batajnica air base 252 and had been organised by the Serbian security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, was the position more or less identical before the war broke out in Bosnia? In other words, was there a similar identical situation in Croatia, while the war was going on in Croatia? In other words, the presence of the JNA in Croatia for sure, but were there also paramilitaries, the same paramilitaries operating in Croatia, before they then concentrated on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I think I indicated, something I already said, the fight -- the campaign in Croatia had begun in June 1991. The same strategy was being used, the same approach, the same mixture of JNA. At that stage, the JNA was remaining as the JNA, both there and in Bosnia. At times it said it was carrying out a peacekeeping operation, but it was essentially assisting this Serbian campaign. Local Territorial Defence units were used and paramilitary forces from Serbia were used as part of that campaign, and the same pattern of surrounding places with armour or heavy artillery and then using the shock troops, or paramilitaries, to go in as part of the strategy to take over and to clear out potential operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. Was there a cease-fire in Croatia at any given moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a cease-fire agreement in Croatia at the beginning of January 1992. That said, the low-level hostilities continued all the way to 1995, and at certain points during 1993, 1994, 1995, there were also significant operations initiated by Croatian forces. But I don't think there was ever a point where there was a genuine, full cease-fire. But there was a cease-fire agreement in January 1992 which led to the deployment of the United Nations force in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there any substantial withdrawal of the JNA forces from Croatia into Bosnia at any given moment after this supposed cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a withdrawal even before the supposed cease-fire agreement, and certainly after it. Again, forces were left in place as the Serbian Territorial Defence of the RSK, which became the army of Serbian Krajina, Vojska Srpksa Krajina. Some of those forces were withdrawn into Bosnia and Herzegovina, as indeed had been earlier forces from Slovenia. When the withdrawal of Slovenia took place, some of those forces went into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you agree that as a result of this withdrawal of JNA forces from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presence of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina was strengthened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might well have been. I think that the plans were already underway for shaping the position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think it's quite likely that would have strengthened the position. It certainly would have left -- some materiel was left in Croatia, some of the materiel was withdrawn and would have then been at the disposal of the forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the JNA otherwise strengthened, apart from the returning forces from Croatia? Was it strengthened in any other way in preparation of the conflict that eventually occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I might -- that I fully understand where you might be going with this. Let me say that the JNA had a position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that as part of the mobilisation, armed forces were being moved out -- this is through the autumn of 1991, armed forces were being moved out of barracks onto permanent exercises. That was part of the way of mobilising Territorial Defence forces to work with them as well. That was doing two things. It was to make sure that the -- that what had happened in Slovenia and in some places in Croatia that JNA forces could not be trapped in barracks, that they would be out in the field and in a position to be used. And it was also ensuring that they were in a position and carrying out exercises in places that might be of key importance so that when the time came - this is my assumption, I can go no further than that - that they were deployed and out and in strength and in their position to take whatever action would be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question is actually based on two things that you mentioned earlier. One was the anticipation on the part of Belgrade that the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was only a matter of time, and secondly, the plans that were put in place by Belgrade for a Serbian state, which would necessarily transborder into parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and which would require definitely the presence of the JNA over there, whichever, so this is -- so would you agree that this would required, first and foremost, the strengthening of the JNA -- of the presence of the JNA in the areas where the Serbs had a particular interest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the JNA was already very strong in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second military district of the JNA became effectively the general staff of the Serbian republic -- the Republika Srpska. It had such a preponderance of weaponry, both in terms of heavy artillery and armour, so outweighing anything else that a strong position was already established. The one thing it lacked was manpower. The manpower, as far as possible, was also to come from the Territorial Defence forces, and later on in the war, at times there would be supplements from Serbia. But because of the situation in Serbia, trying as far as possible to disguise its involvement and not to be too open, the opportunities for doing that were quite limited. So part of this preparation was ensuring that the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina was strong and was in a position to carry out those actions. But the forces used were predominantly those already within Bosnia and Herzegovina, although they were controlled and commanded from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I think we can take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would just ask, I don't know if I could move things into evidence, or as soon as I come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sellers. We'll have a 25-minute break from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. I recognise Mr. Wubben. Have you taken over, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At least to address one issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You asked for the parties to sit down to agree upon a date for oral pleadings, and we did so, and we advise that it will be subsequent to the hearing of Ms. Manas on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Friday. That's perfect. I thank you. Ms. Sellers, before you proceed with tendering some fresh documents in evidence, Judge Eser would like to put two questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to come back to the problem of the ethnic composition. Now, what are the criteria? How can you distinguish between different ethnic compositions? Is it race? Is it religion? Is it the place where people are born or brought up? What are the main criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could begin perhaps an extensive philosophical/social inquiry about that. If you'll permit me to try a shortcut in the first place. When I talk about these issues, it's based on self-definition in the censuses in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1981 and 1991, where people put themselves into categories. Perhaps even there you can see that sometimes ethnicity in those forms of identity have a degree of potential fluidity because the number of Yugoslavs from one point to another, for example -- I forget the exact figure, but it was kind of significantly higher in 1981 than it was in 1991. I don't think that's because a certain group of people disappeared completely, but perhaps it's more likely, can be no more than speculation because we haven't got this specific research, that these people that once said, "I'm a Yugoslav," but in the changing situation and with the pressures upon identity was be defining themselves in some other way, would be a hunch. But for the purposes of the evidence that's given, those are based on the self-definition of the identity as declared those taking part in the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So when you gave some figures, some percentage of the ethnic composition, all these figures are based on self-declaration of the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Built on self-declaration expressed through the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But what would these people consider as relevant for being a member of the one group or the other ethnic group? What are the criteria for themselves to belong to one group or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, quite frankly, without to a point of doing research and interviewing each individual one of -- you could never give a true authoritative answer to that kind of question. I think the elements which are usually taken to form part of this are things to do with culture, to do with the religion underpinning a particular community, perhaps to do with language. Or in the case of language, or languages, as some people say in this part of the world, the particular script that's used, the particular dialect. In the eastern part the Ekavian dialect is used. In the western parts of the region and Ikavian dialect is used. So there are differences of vocabulary. Family loyalty, i.e -- there are many factors which can come into this. I think the only thing that I can say we can take reliably is that this is these how people defined themselves, whatever criteria they used to reach that definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: You mentioned at one point -- before the various referenda, you told us that there had been tension in the ethnic particular fabric. What are the reasons, as you -- as far as you can estimate, reasons for these tensions? Are these shorter tensions, or are they going back to other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were probably three elements. The first is memory, so some kind of memory of an imagination of history. Quite clearly, in some parts of the borderlands, either side of the Croatian and Bosnian border, there were people who still remembered a Second World War, or, rather, there was a second generation who had a memory, what you call a memory of it, people who grew up being told, "Those people over there killed your grandfather. You don't talk to them." I think it's undoubted that there were elements of that. The second element is quite clearly that in the situation of growing political tension in this moment where people were being forced -- in some sense when there's an argument, it's very difficult to stand completely back, especially when you're all involved. So issues between Belgrade and Zagreb could become issues between ethnic Serbs and ethnic Croats in some of these places, and ethnic Slovenes versus ethnic Serbs, perhaps, if it came to that. You know, people -- these events help people think about things. And the third element I should have thought you need to take into account is the atmosphere in the way that the political debate is expressed, not something about -- to which I've spent -- to which I've devoted time particularly. But there are studies, for example, the one by Mark Thompson, "Forging War," on the way in which the press used some of these issues and shaped issues, fostering some of this tension. So I think there is a tension in the fabric which is partly there anyway. Another factor which, you know, not wanting to go too far into the anthropology of it, is social change. In the late 1970s, quite a lot of people moved around in Yugoslavia. There was -- development took place, and one of the things that people have told me, who have lived in places like Tuzla or Sarajevo is that there was a difference when you get the influx in the late '70s of people who have been living elsewhere in the countryside who are not part of the traditional community as well. So, yeah, I can -- I think, you know, certainly those three factors and possibly that fourth one that I would identify as being elements which are playing a part in those tensions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. The second issue I want to address was your description of the defence system. You described the JNA as a first tier and the Territorial Defence as the second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, the Territorial Defence units, did they have uniforms, uniforms different from the JNA, or was it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the JNA was the regular army. It was the standing army. It had an officer corps, and it had a conscript cadre. The conscripts were recruited in proportion to ethnic distribution within the whole of the population of the Socialist Federative Republic of the -- of 18 to 25 year-olds. They would all be wearing the JNA uniform and would be in the army all the time, or all the time during their service. The Territorial Defence, as a second-tier force, was not organised not at the federal level by the federal Ministry of Defence and the army, although obviously it was part of an overall federal defence approach. It was organised, first of all, at the republican level, at the state level, and below that at municipality/community levels. The people who were part of the Territorial Defence would have day jobs. They might well have been judges or academics like yourself and myself, but at some point in the year they would go and take part in Territorial Defence exercises if they were active members of the Territorial Defence force, and they would be expected, in a time of mobilisation, to become part of the Territorial Defence force, and they would -- those who were actively involved would have uniforms. They would have marks of identification. But I think the reality was that some people in these structures of Territorial Defence and civil defence at times didn't have the most up-to-date equipment or -- the system was there in theory, and it was meant to fall back so that everybody would become part of a defence effort, if necessary. But I suspect, from talking to people, that it wasn't always as fully -- as fully kitted out as theory might have expected it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
