utterances.text: Mr. Gow, does the village guards, if you would have to put them in a certain position -- in some of the villages which have been the goal of attacks, there have been village guards. Do they fit into this two-tier system, or are they outside of this two-tier system which you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first I must say I don't have any particular expertise about the villages or village guards, to which I think you're making reference. I'm not sure about to what you're making reference, but I would expect that anybody described as a village guard in the time of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and in this transition, would be somebody who's a part of the Territorial Defence force structure. If you're talking at a later stage, it's quite possible that they could be volunteers within one of developing local or paramilitary movements. Again, without knowing the detail of what you're talking about, I can limit it to saying that I think in times they would be part of it, but it might well depend on the precise situation and what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I might just follow up a question basically brought up by Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you possibly clarify for us if there is a difference between a reservist and a member of the Territorial Defence organisation, or are those two things, reservist and Territorial Defence member, always one and the same thing and we're using interchangeable terms?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's my understanding that for an initial period after service somebody would be designated a reservist, and they could also be expected to be part of the Territorial Defence force. But it would be expected that they would be first mobilised into the JNA in a time of action. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing that I know the answer to, but I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you care to tell me first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- pose the question. Did the TOs have their own weapons, weaponry and ammunition and depots, and where would those usually be located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Territorial Defence forces within each of the states had its own arsenal, and they would be located in Territorial Defence depots distributed around the territory within the republic as a whole, within particular communities, often hidden under mountains, sometimes in particular warehouses. They would have their own designated weaponry, and of course lots of people would also have small weapons, you know, light weapons, at home as well. The idea was that everybody and everything should be mobilised if the need came to defend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did the JNA itself have any authority on the TOs, direct authority, in particular with regard to these weapons, the availability of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In times of war or in times of military occupation, the Territorial Defence forces were supposed to form part of a whole armed force with the JNA, if that was possible. But the assumption built into the defence doctrine was that the initial resistance would not be sustained and so there would be a fall-back position. So as far as possible, each small unit would work with larger units, ensuring also the political military relationship and being subordinate, wherever possible, to whatever the high -- the highest available level of JNA command was. The JNA didn't have technical, formal, legal responsibility over the weaponry of the Territorial Defence forces, which were the property of the republics. But as the overall -- as overall responsible for defence within the federation, at times there were issues and tensions, and one of those points was in the last stages of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia where the JNA went and, in several occasions -- into place -- as the emerging potential for independence came, they went and took weaponry from significant stocks in Slovenia. though the Slovenes managed to hold onto some of it, just most of the stocks in Croatia and within Bosnia-Herzegovina took some things and allowed Bosnian Serbs to take others and redistributed weaponry that they had taken control of. At the time they told republican Territorial Defence authorities that this was part of a programme of renewal. But of course weaponry was taken away and nothing was replaced, because the intention was to try to underpin the coming strategic context by removing arms from some of the potential actors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there, at any given moment before the breaking out of the conflict, any directive from the Ministry of Defence to the TOs, to the various TOs, in Bosnia in particular, to hand over all the weaponry to the JNA for safekeeping by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the same thing, as part of this process, has happened in Croatia and Slovenia. A directive -- there was actually an agreement between representatives of the Bosnian presidency, in particular from the Interior Minister Mr. Delimustafaic, and to the JNA to take weaponry from Territorial Defence forces into JNA protection supposedly for safekeeping as part of an effort, they thought -- this is what they were saying at the time -- to make sure weapons were not available, to limit the possibility for the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Sellers, sorry to have interrupted you for so long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for your interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to go back to something a bit mundane right now, and that would be to ask the registrar for a number for the Prosecution exhibit regarding my view of the breakup, ERN number 00339513. Could I please have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P410.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would move to tender this into evidence. And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is so being admitted, Ms. Sellers, and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P410.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also there is the map that Dr. Gow used. It was already premarked 366. I would like to now move that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which map?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is the map that related to the various places where the outbreak of the war was. It's under section 4 of our binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would also like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it gets number P366.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has already got an exhibit number, or is it being given one now? Oh, I see, I see. So it's being given P366 because it had been premarked already, no? Okay. Ms. Sellers, that document is being admitted in evidence and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P366. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you've testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll raise that. My attention is being drawn to the fact that, as far as P410 is concerned, Exhibit P410 is concerned, we've only got the English text. We do not have the original B/C/S text. So I suppose you will take care of that later on, and it will be incorporated in the same P410.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. We apologise. We put in for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to apologise, Ms. Sellers. Just rectify it, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Will do. You'll also find in the next exhibit that we're about to present that we'll run into the same issue, and I'll say ditto beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you testified not only about General Kadijevic but also about Mr. Jovic. I would ask everyone to turn to section 5 in their binder. Dr. Gow, could you look at this document, ERN number 03022817, and would you please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's a translation of an extract from the published diary extracts of Borisav Jovic, whom I mentioned before was the Serbian representative to the collective state body within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And if you would turn to the page that has the 5th of December, 1991 midway through. Dr. Gow, could you explain the importance, if any, of that statement contained in the diary of Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: This is the diary entry that confirms the things I was saying earlier about the discussions between Jovic and Milosevic and then between Jovic and Kadijevic about preparing to avoid, as far as possible, the accusations against Belgrade of involvement in Bosnia of aggression by reorganising -- by redistributing personnel within the JNA in advance of this. And the date, 5th of December, 1991, shows that that's clearly in advance of the actual recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which came in April. And this was preparation as part of the planning ahead of time to ensure that the Serbian project could both run but also be, as far as possible, non-attributable to Belgrade. And if you turn the page, I think you can also see the December 25th entry is the one that says, "Conversation with Veljko" - "Veljko" refers to Veljko Kadijevic, General Kadijevic - "and Slobodan," Slobodan Milosevic. "Veljko reports that 90 per cent of the military has been dislocated," I think the translation says, it probably means relocated, "in accordance with the 5th of December discussions." So that that action has been taken and that the JNA is predominantly in a position now to be able to separate and to have the armed force to operate in Bosnia while saying that it's a Bosnian Serb force and Belgrade, as far as possible, trying to distance itself and say that it's not involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I would ask that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Are you aware of any United Nations Resolutions, either GA or Security Council, regarding the presence of the JNA in Bosnia before and during the early days of the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would have precisely justified the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was already United Nations attention to this issue in September - Security Council 713 had imposed an arms embargo on the SFRY and all its territories - which had begun a process of international engagement. Well, it continued a process of international engagement already begun by the European Community, as it then was. In January, just after this, this was the UN Security Council resolution to authorise the deployment of the UN peace force to Croatia. Now, clearly at the time this was taking place, it was understood that that was underway that there would the cease-fire agreement under the Vance Plan in Croatia, that force would be deployed, and by this stage I think it was as already clear that the headquarters for that force was going to be based in Sarajevo. The decision to base it in Sarajevo was, in part, I think, a gesture. It doesn't make practical operational sense. It was a gesture to make sure that attention was being paid to Bosnia-Herzegovina in this emerging situation. And already, I think, in November there had been requests from the Bosnian presidency to the UN to become involved and to deploy a preventive force there, for various reasons, the politics of it that didn't develop. And as we move on, when you come to the point after the beginning of armed hostilities, the UN Security Council identifies the presence of other forces there in resolution, I think it's 770, off the top of my head. But I'm sure we can check that for the record. But it identifies the presence of these forces. It declares that their presence is a threat to international peace and security and demands the withdrawal of those forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this was properly identified and anticipated when the decision of redistributing the composition of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was quite clear that the Belgrade leaders had understood what the situation was likely to be and were taking action to adjust to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you mentioned the Serbian project, which is the name of your most recent book. I would like to ask you, the name "Serbian Project," is it similar, is it another way of phrasing what some people refer to as the drive for a Greater Serbia? Could you explain if there is any distinction to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Well, first, I use that term to make some distinctions. I mean, it's a vain hope, at times. But in saying "Serbian project," there's the hope that it's a way of trying to be able to distinguish these events, this political military activity from the Serbian people, the Serbs as a whole. It's a difficult thing to do because people tend to ally things. But one of the things I wanted to do was to say, was to try to identify it with this state project. The term "project" is used in my -- my usage of project is rather than something like plan, because it was something which had aims and objectives but was not a fully worked out plan because it was flexible and adaptable to situations. So within that context, I'm looking at something which is a move to create a set of territories for the Serbs, Serbian states, or one Serbian state, across the region. The idea of Great Serbia is one with historic roots, going back to the nineteenth century. The term that's used, for example, by General Kadijevic is a new Yugoslavia. Other terms were circulating at this time in the 1980s as a federation of Serbian states, an association of Serbian states. Again, part of the element of the flexibility is that it was clear that the aim was to establish an arrangement which involved territories of ethnically -- self-ethnically-defining Serbs and really largely removed of other populations. The idea of Great Serbia is consistent with that, but a Great Serbia is not the only option and the only thing we're talking about. So when people talk about Great Serbia, they are talking about something that is consistent with this, but I prefer to be careful and avoid the use of that term as such most of the time because there were ambiguities and there were different options available. But the aim was to still to create a set of linked territories for -- in the name of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, then am I correct in my understanding that the Serbian project, as you described it, necessarily implies that there might be flexibility in different political stance as well as different military tactics in order to achieve the goal of territorial -- re-designing of territory for Serb people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's -- that's quite clearly the case. It's not too difficult to understand that if the leadership in Belgrade, or indeed some other part of it, said we want to create a Great Serbia, we want to challenge the basic principle of international life, i.e., the inviability of territorial integrity under the principle of sovereignty, they would have been identified as breeching international law in the most clear-cut way and would have been met with responses in the most clear-cut way. At every stage politically and militarily, the efforts were taken to create ambiguity and to disguise so as to try to minimise the clear identification and placing of responsibility on the leadership in Belgrade for the programme that it had generated. Pardon me, which it had generated, but of course had support among ethnic Serbian populations. Yeah. We should always bear in mind that there was support for it. It was not ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to turn a little bit and ask you, what was the Bosnian response to the military attacks that you've described initiated, or certainly with the participation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The Bosnian government in this position began to organise its resistance, to some extent, the political leadership of the predominant -- what's called the Muslim party, it was called the Party of Democratic Action, had already become laying the foundations with something like the Patriotic League in the middle of 1991. But once armed hostilities came following the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent personality, it mobilised the portions of the Territorial Defence force under its control, gave instructions that portions of the -- in theory, all elements of the Territorial Defence force should be under its control, began to shape and form an armed force which was to become the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was initially declared, I think, on the 15th of April. It was later declared again at different stages. These are all parts of an evolving effort to create armed forces on the part of the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also reflecting predominantly the Muslim community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to combat the efforts from the Serbian side, to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to create a territorially separate state. And in that context, the Bosnian presidency sought the support of international actors, asked for further international involvement from the UN Security Council, and eventually there was a UN peace force also deployed to Bosnia. And it also made declarations of war, all part of its efforts to say -- to stand for the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the Serbian attempt to break it up. We should also note, for the record, that on and off at times there was a Croatian attempt from the other side also to breach the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I would like to ask for a number for the diary of Mr. Jovic, if the registrar would please give it. That would be ERN number 03022817, that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P4111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So, Ms. Sellers, the diary is being so admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P411.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like everyone to turn to section 6 in their binder. Dr. Gow, if you could please turn to a document that has been premarked P278. The original, I believe, is in B/C/S, ERN number 00520756. I would like you to turn to the English version of the document that has already been marked P277E. Is it 8? I'm sorry. Dr. Gow, could you inform the Trial Chamber of what this document concerns.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document is an extract from the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated Saturday, the 20th of June, 1992. The particular extract here, clearly highlighted in the middle, notes the declaration by the government of -- the presidency, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina of a state of war. You might also note that the Security Council resolution number I mentioned earlier was not 770. That was the one which actually identified and led to sanctions and the deployment of the forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was 752. And above that you will also notice the identification of the alleged aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, the Yugoslav Army, and the so-called terrorists of the Serbian Democratic Party. And in making this declaration, you can also see further down the page, which has also come up highlighted, that Bosnia and Herzegovina is undertaking, in doing this, to comply with the provisions of international law and other international -- relevant international documents about the conduct of war, while acting both -- claiming to act under Article 51 of the United Nations charter, i.e., exercising the right to self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you also turn the page and tell the Trial Chamber, what is the date of this declaration?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The date of the declaration is also the date that I gave for the Official Gazette, which is the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. This document has already been premarked. I would also ask that it be tendered into evidence, if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, so it will be 278, no?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be 278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this document, which has already been premarked, is being admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P278. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in addition to the declaration of independence, did the newly formed Republic of Bosnia have to concern itself with self-defence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It did, as I think I just pointed out. The declaration made reference to the Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, about exercising the right to self-defence. In seeking to exercise that right to self-defence, as I said, they set about forming armed forces, using existing Territorial Defence structures. If you follow on -- actually, on the page you had before, the subsequent thing is about an order for general mobilisation to take people into the Territorial Defence forces, saying that all able and active people should be mobilised at that moment generally into the Territorial Defence force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So therefore the newly formed Republic of Bosnia tended to keep the structure, or possibly that it had inherited from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: They were turning to the Territorial Defence force structures, as far as they were available to it, that had been part of the defence system within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I think we have to recognise that parts of the Territorial Defence system were taken over and acquired by the Serbian side and parts were taken over by the Bosnian side, although the Bosnian authorities sought formally to exercise control over all of them. In principle, they argue they should control all of them. De facto, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you now to turn to the following document. It has been marked -- premarked already 277. The ERN number is 00480501. Dr. Gow, I would like to ask you to look at the English version of that document, and that has been premarked 277E. The ERN number is 00607094. Dr. Gow, could you please inform the Trial Chamber the importance, if any, of this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document, again, is from the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this time from a month earlier, the 20th of May, and it's publishing, as you can clearly read, lawful regulation act of the armed force of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the law on the armed forces. This is the law which regulates the use of the armed forces, and it's a law which is then used as the basis for creating and structuring an army at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I please draw your attention to Article 16 of this document, Dr. Gow. Could you, in your expert opinion, inform the Trial Chamber of whether the different units that would constitute the army of the Republic of Bosnia would include TO units, reserve units, or other units of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: If we understand that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as such, didn't really exist at this stage, it was in a phase of transition, that the Territorial Defence force was being used as the basis for action but also as a way of working towards forming an army, then I think you can say that the Territorial Defence force, in some ways, was becoming the army, but the army would be different from it. And the assumption was that there would still be elements of Territorial Defence, here identified as reservists, all of which would still, in time of war or overriding military exercise, become part of one overall defence framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Until any such army formed for the Republic of Bosnia, then would it be true to say that the Territorial Defence and, as mentioned here, the reserve units would be considered the fighting forces for the political entity of Bosnia that had recently declared its independence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it would. My assumption has always been that, although formally the Bosnian authorities in Sarajevo were declaring an armed force, it was clear that the armed force, as such, was not developed and organised at this stage. Indeed, you could even argue that by the end of armed hostilities in 1995, it was still not fully formed and organised. But at this stage, clearly it was not, and de facto if not formally de jure, but I think also you'd say in terms of the law de jure, defence action was taking place wherever it was possible throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Bosnian authorities' terms, and at a local level, using the pattern, the structure, the doctrine of the defence system, of the old defence system, the All People's Defence doctrine. So at local levels, where possible. But it was a fluid and emerging situation, while they were trying to put a structure together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, because exactly, I'm just appealing to you now to bring everything into proper perspective. The fighting started immediately after the declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that takes us back to April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fighting actually started on the 27th of March, in advance of that. But it's usually said to be April, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until then, was the JNA present in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until then and after then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the formal dissolution of the JNA at that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the creation of the VRS, which supposedly was operative on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which was effectively the ghost of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now, this decision here is date the 20th of May, exactly the day after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The day after the coming into existence officially of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there was already a state of war, in effect; a state of war, without any declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should say that that's true. I mean, the declaration of war itself -- of a state of war by Bosnia and Herzegovina also came a month later than that, but there were armed hostilities underway from the 27th of March at the latest, and those armed hostilities involved, on the one side, forces fighting for the Serbian project and on the other side, those resisting it on the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But as you said, Bosnia -- the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared a state of war a month later, in June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we're here a month earlier, where there was, for all intents and purposes, a state of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armed hostilities were under way. I exercise caution there. I assume that the Bosnian government also declared a state of war for formal, political and legal purposes. I wouldn't want to go into that. I think it's clear that there can be a technical distinction between formal war and armed hostilities, and I would -- if we're taking war in the sense of generically describing armed hostilities, that's fine. I tend to prefer to say armed hostilities because it leaves open other questions that are not ones -- that I think are relevant to my evidence of settling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you see any particular reason why this -- such -- a decision was not taken before, or why it had to wait until the creation of the VRS? Well, I think it's all -- I think -- I mean, we have to understand that things evolve. I think it was -- I already said, I think, that it was the 15th of April that the Bosnian presidency declared the formation of an army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think any time you kind of -- which things you need to do, in terms of political procedure, to create things and to give things a legal basis. I would assume that part of it is just the time in which people are working out the things they need to do that would be good for them to do. Bear in mind also the context of the discussions of the United Nations Security Council, which also at this point I think on the 18th of May, was the 752 resolution, which defined the threat to international peace and security and these issues, so also these actions probably have to be read-- all of this interacting evolve in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, then, would it then be your expert opinion that the hostilities of the armed conflict that occurred on the territory of Bosnia since March were the same hostilities and armed conflict that continued after the signing not only of the declaration of independence, but the formation of the Yugoslav army? Are we talking about a continuous type of armed hostility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In my judgment, there is one armed conflict running from June 1991 that embraces Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I see both of them as parts of one theatre. They're part of the same overall aims and objectives. To create this set of territories, the same approach is used. So in that sense, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the 27th of March, certainly; but it's part of an armed conflict that I see running from the middle of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I just clarify, you've mentioned the date from the 27th of March, 19 --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Which is the date of the first action in Bosanski Brod in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is around a week -- it's actually 10 days before the formal international recognition of Bosnia as independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So armed hostilities from that date on, certainly through till June 20 of 1992, are a continuous form of the armed hostility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Personally, the 20th of June, 1992 makes no difference to what I would describe empirically as the fact of armed hostilities. It may make a difference in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Sorry, the 20th of June declaration might make a difference in other ways, but it doesn't make a difference to the fact of armed hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask the registrar, recognising that we do have P278 and 278E for the English translation, that we keep that and, Your Honour, if I could tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will have Exhibit number P277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, as pointed out by the registrar, that document is being admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P277. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you could, would you describe some of the key elements or the key features of this armed conflict that we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I think the key -- the key, core elements of it are the clash of statehood projects, as I said before, either seeking to preserve states within their previously defined territorial boundaries, or creating new borders; using the strategy of what is described as ethnic cleansing to prosecute the campaign to create new territories, that is, the forcible removal -- in some cases through killing; in others through demonstrative violence in others; through forcible expulsion; in others through intimidation to incite flight, so that there would be no potentially hostile populations on the territory to come under control of those seeking to create this set of states. So ethnic cleansing, the strategy of ethnic cleansing with the character of atrocities and the large outflows of populations, demographic displacement that takes place, is perhaps the key defining element of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And your use of the term "ethnic cleansing," does "ethnic" relate to the different ethnic groups that you testified about when we were actually describing the composition of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It does. And it was an approach initially used by Serbian forces as part of this campaign, but I think we also recognise that it was used at times by other parties to the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- you know, mimicking fashion. I don't know how you would describe it. It was something used and copied by others afterwards. If wasn't exclusively Serbian. But it was the Serbian thrust in the first place which defined the conflict and gave it this character.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you describe ethnic cleansing as both a military and political tactic or --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: It's -- ethnic cleansing is the strategy. Strategy is the point at which politics meets the use of armed force. So strategy is about the creation and application of armed force, of destructive armed force, of violence for political purpose. The aim was to create a set of territories that would be linked and would be Serbian. The political aim within that, which also becomes part of the strategy, is to ensure that there are no potentially hostile populations that area. It's quite clear from the things we've said earlier about the political tensions, the inter-ethnic, inter-communal tensions, that if Serbia takes over territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina with mixed populations, if it takes over areas with mixed populations in Croatia, there will be dissent. At a minimum, there will be political resistance. It's quite likely that there could be political violence, whether it's very low-scale terrorist what we call action or whether it's a larger guerilla action. You remove the potential in terms of -- in security operation terms for that resistance if you remove the population. So you remove an ethno-national group as such and you remove an ethno-national group as a potential challenge to the security situation, as a potential instrument -- source of violent resistance. If I could indulge a little further, I don't want to take time. But in terms of guerrilla doctrine, one of the most famous says is that of Mao Tse-Tung who described the guerrilla as a fish in water. This kind of resistance depends on having a community from which you operate. If in terms of strategy from the Serbian or others using it perspective, you're seeking to remove potential opposition, what you do essentially is remove the water. You remove the population, you remove the support and basis for any violent resistance. So that is the essence. It's political and it's military, and it's combined in the strategy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there reaction by international humanitarian institutions, and more specifically the International Committee of the Red Cross, to the atrocities or the ethnic cleansing that you have just testified about during this armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: There was widespread international attention to what was taking place. The reports of atrocities, the vast outflows of population groups, either within -- from one area of Bosnia and Herzegovina to another, but also refugees moving outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina drew attention to this, the UNHCR drew attention. We have also mentioned the attention of the UN Security Council. The ICRC as an agency, particularly involved in these situations, also gave it attention, and working with other international actors, sought to gain agreement with the parties of the conflict to uphold international standards and to desist from these actions, which they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honours and the witness and Defence counsel please to turn to section 8 of your binders. The ERN number is 00317897 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document, Dr. Gow. Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what is the origin and the nature of this document that you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document is an agreement organised by the ICRC to which the parties -- the parties signing are representatives of the different political parties within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's from the 22nd of May, 1992. That's, again, in the context we've been discussing of the Security Council resolution on the 18th of May, 1992, the general international attention being given to Bosnia and Herzegovina because of the large-scale problems of atrocity there. And as part of an international effort, I think, to see this, there was an attempt to get the political representatives of the parties to sign an agreement undertaking to uphold the elements of international humanitarian law relating to armed conflict, in particular the third convention of the Geneva Conventions, which is common to all four Geneva Conventions, but also additionally getting them to recognising aspects of the Geneva Convention ... The Geneva Conventions that wouldn't necessarily be agreed upon by all parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to draw your attention to the names that have been signed at the top part of the document, and to explain that they've been signed on behalf, as representatives of other persons. Could you please tell us who these other political or otherwise persons are, whom they're representing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I can tell you. We can read in front of us that Mr. Trnka is representing the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic. The president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is also a member of the Party of the Democratic Action, the Muslim party within Bosnia. Mr. Kalinic is representing Radovan Karadzic, who is the representative of the Serbian Democratic Party, as is also Mr. Djogo. Mr. Kurjak signs as representative of Mr. Izetbegovic, not as president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but as the president of Party of Democratic Action. So both Karadzic and Izetbegovic have two representatives. One is in there, what they take as their formal office, and one is there as leaders of political parties. And finally, Mr. Sito Coric is a representative of Mr. Brkic on behalf of the Croatian Democratic Community, which is the predominantly ethnic Croat party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, are all of the signatories representing the division of ethnic groups within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: They represent the main ethnically defined parties within Bosnia and Herzegovina. We could just for the record be clear. We didn't say earlier that within Bosnia and Herzegovina we had these groups. There were also people who were not -- didn't define themselves either as Muslims or Serbs or Croats. Somewhere in the region of 11 per cent of the population in the last census didn't define themselves as one of those three things. Some were Jews, some were others, some were Yugoslavs. But just to be clear. But these were the three main ethnic groups, and these were the representatives of the three main political parties representing those groups, who were also the ones engaged politically within the context of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: In connection with your description that certain people declared themselves as Serb or Bosnian Muslim or something else, how was it in the connection with the ethnic cleansing? Would it have been possible that the person would say, "From now on, I would define myself differently"? Or was it the case, if you declared yourself at one time to be a Serb, you remained it all your life or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very interesting question, because I think certainly it's theoretically possible that somebody could redesignate themselves, and I'm not sure whether some people redesignated themselves as such. But there have been points in cases in other Trial Chambers here where someone has been described both as a member of one ethnic community but also as part of another or acting for another. One that springs to mind, if I recall it correctly, is that of Drazen Erdemovic. Yeah, so in some ways not quite understanding the process and the motivations, that can happen. Perhaps more significantly, I think, we should say that part of the procedure of ethnic cleansing was that documentation was prepared and available, and from the outset, as part of a scheme. This included documents where either people, in some cases, could sign over property rights and buy a one-way exit visa and so forth. But in other cases, they could also sign something to accept the new regime and to define themselves, whether ethnically or not, as loyal to this situation, and if not defining themselves ethnically with the dominant group in whichever area it was, could at least stay where they were as second-class citizens. And despite the ethnic cleansing in many -- there were places where even, by the end of the whole period, it was -- there were still some areas where it wasn't completely purely sorted out in ethnic terms. So I think that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So could you draw the conclusion that objects or victims of ethnic cleansing have been those people who stayed with their former self-declaration as X or Y, but if somebody would say, "Now, from now on, I would take a different position, I would not become victim of ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there's the possibility there. I think we have to be cautious in saying anything as a complete generalisation in the nature of that kind of problem where it's about self-definition and other definition. I don't know of a case, but I think it's hypothetically possible that there could be a person -- hypothetically take the example of Serbian forces taking over a place and expelling Muslims, that it's hypothetically possible that somebody could define themselves perhaps as a Serb, self-definition for whatever reason, but are identified by others as a Muslim, might say, "No, really, I'm a Serb," but then still be subject to ethnic cleansing because of the other perception. The censorship information can come through self-definition. In the context of operations of ethnic cleansing and politics, I think we have to take into account also the role of other definition and the interaction and exercise a bit of caution and probably not draw any absolute conclusion, but maybe identify general tendencies or likelihoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could we concluded that it was two elements in it conclusions, self-declaration by the person concerned and description of a certain type, social description to be a member of this group or that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're talking about the context in which we're looking at operations pursuant to the strategy, yes. If we're talking about the information in the census, then that's about self-description and not about the ascription by others. So just to be clear. If we're talking about the information from the census, then that's about self-description. But in the context -- in other context, particularly that of operations, pursuant to the strategy, then there's the element of other ascription as well as self-definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps one could add at this point, Judge Eser, because your question was a very relevant and a very important one, one could add also that -- and correct me if I'm wrong, Dr. Gow, that the social background to it all is that in these small villages, in particular, the villages themselves were classified as almost entirely Muslim, entirely Serbian, and everyone -- this is a society where, leaving apart the big cities, otherwise everyone knew everyone else. The names themselves, most of the time, not the surname, not the family name, but the names themselves would identify you as rather of Muslim extraction or -- I mean, the Croats had special -- typical Croatian names, the Muslims typical Muslim names, and sometimes even family names. But this is a society which is very typical of the region. Everyone knows everyone else, so there is no way one could be mistaken for a Serbian when it was actually a Muslim, for example, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's largely true when you're talking about local actors. But in some cases where you're looking at paramilitary forces coming in from Serbia, they wouldn't necessarily know the first thing about the area. But they also would have relied already on local organisation within this SDS and security-service organised crisis headquarters to identify those members of the local community who should be in the first range of targets to be removed. I think I should also say, if I may pursue that a little further, that some villages probably would be predominantly with one community or another. Some might be almost entirely one community. Most probably would be mixed. But the research of anthropologists shows there were parallel communities, so they would live side by side. They would know each other without necessarily that degree of mixing. And on the names, what you said would be true to a large extent, but there are also names which could occur in any one with those categories, and you wouldn't necessarily know by the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as far as appearance and physiognomy is concerned, you couldn't actually distinguish between one ethnic group and another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think broadly that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've cleared that terrain at least, so we don't need to return to it later on. Yes, Ms. Sellers. Again my apologies to you for interrupting you so often, which is not my style. But at the same time, I think I'm anticipating some pleasures yet to come, and I'm preparing for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think we're advancing as a whole, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So My apologies to you, and please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would ask you to draw your attention to section 2.3 of the ICRC document, the subsection entitled "Civilian Population." In that section there's a reference to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949. What is your understanding that the Geneva Conventions of 1949 govern?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: They govern international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you testified earlier --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Sorry, with the exception of Article 3, which I already -- I think you already said earlier is common to all four conventions and applies to non-international armed conflict as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would this document seem to want to encourage the different signatories to abide by the law of war that governs both international war and non-international war?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The document clearly gets the parties within Bosnia and Herzegovina to accept the application of Common Article 3, and in addition that, in the area you have here is to note that civilian populations have protected status and to apply elements of international armed conflict beyond Common Article 3 to the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask you now to turn to section 2.5 of the document, and it is the sub-entitled "Conduct of hostilities." There there's a reference to Additional Protocol I. In your understanding, what does Additional Protocol I regulate in terms of international law?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: While recognising that although I have a significant interest in these matters of international law, I am not, as such, an international lawyer, my understanding is that Additional Protocol I was agreed by those who took part to enhance the provisions of international armed -- of international humanitarian law relating to armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask the registrar, could we please have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, It will be P412.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this document is being admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P412. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, did the JNA withdrawal from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina occur in a manner which they completely withdrew forces, equipment, logistics, or any other military equipment or apparatus?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I think to reiterate some things that we've said before, I think "withdrawal" is not completely the right word. Although that is the one that was used to described what happened, it wasn't about withdrawal. It was about division of the JNA into the VRS and the VJ, that is the Bosnian Serb military and the military of Serbia Montenegro. So in that process, the assets and the personnel of the JNA deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, small exception, I think there were a few non-Bosnian Serb people who withdrew at that point, was that -- sorry. The JNA was divided, and part of the JNA that was left in Bosnia and Herzegovina as the VRS. So the withdrawal -- "withdrawal" is the wrong term. The bulk of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina was left behind and redesignated as the VRS. And not only was it left there, but it continued to have links to Serbia and Montenegro, to Belgrade. It was -- the commander, General Ratko Mladic, was given significant operational authority and command, but was reported as being in regular contact with the staff in Belgrade. The Belgrade military continued to give all kinds of support, being part of one integrated structure, throughout the period of armed hostilities and indeed beyond armed hostilities. Even to this day, there are still some issues about trying to get the separation of the integration of the armed forces as part of a process of security sector forming Serbia Montenegro and in the Serbian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What would you give as the date of, on the one hand, possibly the misnomer of the withdrawal of the JNA and, on the other hand, the formation of the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The 19th of May, 1992, was the date given by Belgrade to say -- that was the date by which it said it would withdraw the JNA. But, as I say, it didn't withdraw the JNA. It simply transformed the JNA into two parts. So the 19th of May is the date on which the JNA ceases to exist and, by relation, on which I think we can say the VRS and the VJ come into being.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how does this withdrawal compare to the JNA withdrawal from Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The JNA withdrawal from Slovenia, first of all, was a withdrawal. It was a withdrawal which raised the territory that it went. Anything that couldn't be withdrawn was destroyed, was ruined, so that it couldn't be left as an acquisition to Slovenia and be used. That came after a three-month moratorium, and those forces, as we've said earlier, went into Bosnia-Herzegovina initially. The withdrawal from Croatia has two dimensions. On the one hand, the withdrawal from non-Serbian-controlled parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina shares characteristics with those from Slovenia. All assets were withdrawn, and anything that couldn't be moved, physical assets, things that were immobile, would be ruined to put them beyond use. In contrast, the withdrawal from Croatia -- from Serbian-controlled areas in Croatia, again, bequeathed equipment and capability to the VSK, the Republika Srpska Krajina so-called armed forces. If you contrast that again, in fact, also with the withdrawal from Macedonia, where there was an agreement between Belgrade, military and political, to withdraw from Macedonia in the south, there was a complete withdrawal. But again, everything that couldn't be taken was ruined and left behind. So we see a clear difference in the pattern. Bequeathing personnel and equipment, materiel, capability to the Serbian forces in the Serbian-controlled areas, and withdrawing everything and destroying that which cannot be withdrawn in the other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak a bit about the weaponry that the JNA left in Bosnia, the weaponry that, if I understand correctly, you're saying was bequeathed to the VRS. Could you inform the Trial Chamber a bit about the nature of that weaponry.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: When we say that there was this division of the armed forces and the VRS came into being, it came into being with almost all the weaponry that was at the disposition of the second military district command of the old JNA. Some elements of the air force, the most advanced and sophisticated elements, were taken to Serbia. But other elements, the older planes, the guards were left to operate with the forces of the VRS normally. The inheritance included something like 1.000 pieces of artillery. Similarly large numbers of pieces of armour, tanks, armoured vehicles. So there was a preponderance, what in some places I've called a superabundance of weaponry on the Serbian side, which pitched against the things we said earlier about removal of weaponries from Territorial Defence forces for the Bosnian authorities, and generally the situation in which the Bosnian government found itself -- remember, there was a kind of clear imbalance in terms of weapons categories, because most of the big weapons were on one side and far fewer of them were on the other, which meant that, in the broad, strategic picture, the Serbian forces were able to dominate the environment where they were able to operate using these capabilities. They were limited, I should point out, by a relative lack of manpower. So they had all the weaponry, but they couldn't make as much use of it as they could have done because of having this more than 1.000 kilometre front line. But it enabled them to dominate and hold the situation strategically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, for a point of clarification, when you refer in that instance to the use of the military weapons by the Serbians, are you referring to the Bosnian Serbs or, more specifically, the VRS army in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I'm talking about the VRS. I would also generally assume that within that, there would be moments where the VJ was also part of the picture and contributing at times. But we're talking about the Bosnian Serb military, the VRS, the inheritance that it had in terms of weaponry and the way in which that weaponry was used to prosecute the project, the campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And your reference to the VJ, would you please inform Your Honours what you mean by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The army of Yugoslavia; that is, the army of Serbia and Montenegro, Vojska Yugoslavia

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was that basically the renaming of what we had been calling the JNA, as it went back into the territory of the remaining republic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: That's the name of the armed force for which Belgrade is the political and military command and control, the state -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro. When the JNA is divided, part of it becomes the VRS, the other part becomes the VJ. The VRS in Bosnia, with the Bosnian Serbs; the VJ with Serbia and Montenegro on the other side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you now to turn to section 9 in your binder, and you will note that there is a map. Dr. Gow, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you do this, perhaps we can close on the part that you've been dealing with. Now, we have, for all intents and purposes, the JNA disappearing as such. It's being divided into two, according to you. One is the VRS and the other is the VJ. As far as the command structure, starting from the 19th of May - I'm only interested in the 19th of May and afterwards - the command structure, where did it start and where did it end, as far as the VRS is concerned, as far as the VJ is concerned? Because obviously then it becomes very important for us to know with regard to the operations that followed, where they were being planned, where they were being conducted, managed, whether it was in one state or whether it was in another part of that state. That's the first part I would like you to elucidate. The second is, do you mean to tell us that at any given moment after the declaration of independence of Bosnia, or even a few days before, that the -- if the Bosnian government wanted to create its own army, it had to start from scratch, or did it have at its disposal either manpower or resources and also weaponry which was, strictly speaking, part of the JNA? I suppose you can answer. I'm asking you this because I suppose you know, as much as I do and many others, that there was also an arms embargo put in place by the United Nations. So perhaps if you can touch on these two points, separate issues, I think we could close that chapter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In terms of -- I'll start with the Bosnian side of that first and with the arms embargo. I already mentioned earlier in testimony that Security Council Resolution 713 in September 1991 imposed an arms embargo on the SFRY and its territories. The consequence of that, of course, was partly that, in a situation such as that, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with extensive materiel on the Serbian side, with the Territorial Defence structures having been largely, probably not completely, stripped of assets on the Bosnian side, there was this big imbalance. The arms embargo was one of the big political issues at the time said to affect the strategical situation. It did so to the extent that the VRS had all of this heavy weaponry, and the Bosnian army, as it developed, did not. It did have some, most of that which it got it captured in northern Bosnia. But it had something like 40 tanks and armoured vehicles, not to compare with the kind of hundreds, going up to towards 1.000 on the Serbian side. So it couldn't compete on the same terms. But part of the strategy perhaps was to try and gain weaponry as far as possible. The arms embargo was set to cement this situation because, of course, the Bosnian government would want to acquire weapons of other kinds and didn't do so, at least not extensively and formally. It did acquire quite a considerable amount over time of man-portable weaponry, so things that one person could carry, including rocket launchers and so forth, but not -- but not heavy artillery and armour. It was also capable of producing some things. Some areas, I would say in Central Bosnia, there were still arms factories from the old defence system which were under Bosnian control and where they could still manufacture some capabilities such as elements of artillery and multiple launch systems. So in that picture, there was a big imbalance. There were ways in which the Bosnian side, in trying to develop this army and using initially the structures of the Territorial Defence force, sought to do this. Is that adequate for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, what I wanted to clarify by my question, that part of the question, at least, was - and you have more or less answered it, as expected - that one wouldn't be able to say that the outbreak of these hostilities, the Bosnian government, or the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had or could have at its disposal any substantial weaponry which belonged to the JNA at the time. So you're ruling that out. The bulk of the weaponry was in the hands of the VRS, what eventually became the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The only weaponry at that time was weaponry that it captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: In terms of the command structure. Let me be clear, as far as I can be. The VRS/VJ division is a political division and is a formal one. It does have operational and organisational consequences. One of those, the key one, is that General Mladic, who is already the commander of the second military district, becomes commander of the VRS, has -- is given broad operational authority. He's in charge of the operations in Bosnia. He has -- he still has links to Belgrade, and I think it's also worth bearing in mind, we should never forget, we don't have a map to show it, but Han Pijesak, in Eastern Bosnia, was the old deep underground command and control centre for the JNA, remained in Eastern Bosnia notionally under the command of the JNA, but was the core of this integrated JNA defence system. That continued to be part of the links with Belgrade. So Belgrade was giving -- was setting the political agenda strategically, was creating the framework through the JNA into the divided -- formally divided VJ and VRS. The Chief of Staff in Belgrade, General Perisic, was liaising in part of the chain of command with General Mladic. But because of the issues we discussed before about trying to avoid any sense of -- as far as possible, any sense of identification of Belgrade, trying to project the idea that this was Bosnian Serb rather than Belgrade-generated Serbian activity, Mladic was given authority to run operations and not to be seeking new orders all the time. He would go to Belgrade for meetings -- he was reported as going to Belgrade for meetings. There was one point in 1993 where people expected that he would become the new Chief of Staff of the then VJ as part of all of this. That didn't happen for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Commander-in-Chief, absolute Commander-in-Chief of the two --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The theoretical commander-in-chief of the VJ is the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That comprises the president of Montenegro, the president of Serbia, and the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The theoretical Supreme Commander of the VRS is the president of the Republika Srpksa, who was Mr. Radovan Karadzic. I tend to think that the theoretical political command of the president of the Republika Srpska is, at best, a grey and complex area because the real chain of command through the armed forces, in terms of the strategy, leads to Belgrade. And I think there were times when Karadzic had little idea, probably, of what was going on in terms of the military and Mladic and the operations, and there were a few moments where -- interactions with some militarisations where Karadzic tried to assert his authority and was not very effective in doing so. So I think that's an indication that the real line of authority was within the military and the chain of command going back to Belgrade, and the fact that requests would be sent to Belgrade for extra units to support for equipment, for ammunition, are all elements of the way in which that was one integrated structure working. And as I think I indicated, even after the end of -- formal end of armed hostilities in 1995, that continued to be an issue. The people overseeing the arms control elements of the separation of forces continued to report the difficulties, because there was the integration between Belgrade and the VRS meant that some of the issues that this Republika Srpska was supposed to deal with couldn't be dealt with unless they were dealt with in Belgrade. It meant that, as I say, even today, as people looking to try and bring Serbia into the European fold, take it towards the European Union if it wants to do that at some stage, towards NATO, the issues of security sector reform in Bosnia and sorting this out in Bosnia and in Belgrade are still problematic because of the continuing links, the integration of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sellers, will you be asking at any point, the witness, with regard to possible withdrawals of paramilitaries from Bosnia? Because if you're not, I will pose the question now myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Be my guest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We take it that, or at least you hinted at it, that apart from the regular armed forces, there were also paramilitary groups active in the area, going back even to the Croatian -- conflict in Croatia. Apart from the purported withdrawal of JNA -- of the JNA from Bosnia, and apart from the separation, the practical separation of the JNA into two parts, were there any steps taken with regard to paramilitaries that were present in the territory of Bosnia throughout -- during this period? Did they remain there? Were they withdrawn? Did they withdraw themselves? Can you enlighten us on this.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The paramilitary forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm referring to paramilitaries originating from outside of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Yes, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's keep it to that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: We're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The paramilitary forces organised by Belgrade were not used or kept in any one place for a particularly long time anyway. They were an element of attacks. So in the process of a takeover, the JNA elements of the Bosnian Serb, say, Territorial Defence force might be used to surround a town, a village, a community, to cut it off, operate, perhaps, stand off bombardment. Then it would be -- but they wouldn't have the kind of personnel to go into these places to do these things. So the paramilitaries would provide a kind of shock troop in that situation. There were a variety of paramilitary groups, some organised semi-privately, all of them coordinated by the security service and by the air force intelligence service at Batajnica, who would then go into particular places. But they wouldn't be in any one place for a particularly long time anyway. In some of them, the semi-private operations, one of the motivations for people to join was pillage, so you would be recruited, and sometimes people were given a choice to come out of prison, it's said -- you know, you can stay in prison or you can go and take your chances as part of this unit, but then you can take home whatever booty, whatever goods you can find. There used to be cartoons of vans coming back from Bosnia with lorries loaded up with fridges and so forth, because they were -- these people were semi-criminal. They were part -- they were involved in the ethnic cleansing activity but were then taking things away. So they didn't stay, in some cases, very long anyway, because the part -- for some of them, part of the motive was to do something, get something, and go back and not be in prison anymore, or to continue whatever their life was. So I think to understand, the issue of withdrawal is that these forces were never in any one place very long. So the issue of withdrawal, in a sense, is maybe not completely a non-issue but is not really there as an issue, because they would come and go on raiding missions but wouldn't necessarily be permanently based in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did they continue to come and go even after the partition of the JNA -- after the 19th of May, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, they would continue to be used through 1992. They ceased to be -- they appear to have ceased to have been used in significant ways openly after late 1992, maybe sometime in -- early in 1993. Off the top -- you want it, I could go and kind of gauge exactly when this was. But that was the point at which the position was more or less static. There was a sense that it wasn't changing very much, and would only change slowly. There was no longer, if you like, a need for these shock troops to be involved in taking over places. And at the same time as far as extra resources were needed, they would be supplied from Belgrade by the interior ministry security service, and it would more likely be units of the JSO, the special operations unit of the security service within the interior ministry, the people who organised the paramilitaries in the first place, and sometimes -- and often the JSO members were parts of the some of the groups. So I think it's going back to that structure, to Belgrade, to the command under -- under Mr. Simatovic, who was responsible in Belgrade for organising these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the conclusion to draw, according to you, is that post-19th May, Belgrade was still very much present both as far as the regular army of Republika Srpska is concerned and also the presence, intermittent presence of paramilitary groups operating in the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Sellers, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to Section 9 in your binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to take a break now? Let's have a break. We'll have a break of 25 minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask that the witness, Dr. Gow, counsel, and Your Honours turn to the next document in your binder. It's a document of a map that's been premarked P367.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please look at the map and tell the Trial Chamber: Did you instruct the Prosecutor, I believe it's in 1994, possibly 1995, to develop the map that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I did ask for a map of this kind to be drawn up. I don't know whether it was 1994 or 1995 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the significance of this map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: The map shows the overall control of territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina as it would have been through most of the period from spring 1992 through to 1993. The actual information on which it was based was taken from December 1993, but the position was static for most of that period. The one thing that did change within it was that, what you see on -- what I have here is a black and white map. I'm not sure if we have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There is one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I see the colour. The blue on the screen, for one part of 1993 kind of went towards where those two little blue areas are, more in the center of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the green. That was when Bosnian and Croatian forces were pushed into central Bosnia, fighting against the Muslims, the Bosnian army forces. But then they were pushed back by the end of that year. So for all but a few months, that represented the picture. I should also point out another of the problems of map production in the Prosecutor's Office in the early days of the Tribunal, I suspect, is that again, the area marked in green that includes Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde on this map should not be one unified area. There should be three separate green areas around them. Gorazde was the largest, Zepa the smallest, and Srebrenica a little larger than Zepa, so they shouldn't be joined up in that way on the map. If you can read red into -- red gaps into them. And on the map showing overall control of territory, blue represents Croat control, green represents Bosnian government control, and red represents Serbian control. So in terms of what we were saying before the recess about the dominant Serbian position that was secured, you'll see that probably something in the region of two-thirds of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is under Serbian control through that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Sorry, I'd just add for clarity and for the record. I was asked earlier about the Posavina Corridor and pointed to Brcko. You will see in the north-east corner, towards the top of the map, Brcko marked, and the red line of that corridor, just for sake of fullness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, looking at the map, would you agree that the political and the military division shown on this map followed along ethnic lines in Bosnia during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I would. The intention was to create -- on the Serbian side and also, I think, on the Croatian side at least, ethnically homogeneous territories. So the idea was to create this part of the Serbian state construct of the project and, as far as possible, to remove other groups from that territory. That was the means of consolidating control of the territory, of implementing the strategy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were the different designations in terms of the armies and the ethnic breakdown then the result of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow the question. I mean, I don't think that the designations of the armed forces were a result of ethnic cleansing. I think that ethnic cleansing was the strategy, and this disposition of territory was certainly the outcome of that process of ethnic cleansing, using artillery and heavy armour to create the framework for it, but then also using -- implementing the strategy at the local level, at the low level, using means that included paperwork but also small arm and violence, because that's the point at which you execute it. You don't use the artillery -- the artillery creates the framework, makes the overall control possible. The ethnic cleansing comes from those units on the ground which go to places and either kill or forcibly remove people or process them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Therefore, it would be your testimony that in terms of weaponry, you've already testified about heavy artillery, but now that probably smaller artillery also played a role within the ethnic cleansing strategy that you discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW
utterances.text: Without a doubt. The actual ethnic cleansing is carried out either at the point of a rifle or a sub-machine-gun or a bayonet. The reports in some places like Bijeljina, where people were put into the community hall and knives were used to cut things from people.
